generatedProse.concept-context: In psychology, writing is how most of your work is assessed, from lab reports to essays, and it rewards a staged process rather than a single sitting. A strong psychology essay is planned, drafted and then revised: the first version gets your reading and your argument onto the page, and later passes sharpen them. Treating a psychology assignment as something that must come out right first time makes it far harder than it needs to be.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two psychology students given the same essay to write.

Tom opens a blank document and tries to write the finished essay from the first sentence onwards, polishing each line before moving on. Hours pass, little is written, and what is there cannot be changed without starting again. Tom is treating writing as a single performance that must be perfect first time. This is the harder way.

Amara starts by noting what the question is really asking, jots a rough plan of the main points and the studies she will use, then writes a quick first draft without worrying about how it sounds. With a whole draft to work with, she goes back and improves it: reordering points, sharpening sentences, fixing errors. Amara is treating writing as a process. This is the easier way, and the better essay.

Both students spent the same time. Only Amara used it as a process, turning a blank page into a draft and a draft into a finished piece.
generatedProse.summary: Academic writing in psychology is a process, not a single act of getting it right first time: you understand the task, plan, draft, and then revise. You can now describe those stages and recognise the process in how a student approaches a psychology essay. The next lesson turns the process into practice: understanding the task, planning, and getting a first draft down.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's approach more effective than Tom's?

items.text: She worked in stages - planning, drafting, then revising - rather than trying to write it perfectly first time.
She typed faster than Tom did.
She waited until she could write perfect sentences before starting.
She wrote the whole essay in a single sitting.

feedback.correct: That's right. Amara planned, drafted and then revised, rather than trying to be perfect first time.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara DID differently, that is, working in stages.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara was more effective because she worked in stages. Speed, waiting for perfect sentences, or one long sitting are not it.
